title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
dek: Half the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of those businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
why: A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" back from the tech narrative to regional middle-market businesses. High information density, suited to anyone who cares about tax, PE and wealth distribution.
who: Investors and founders who care about US tax policy, wealth distribution, PE and search funds, and regional middle-market businesses; anyone who wants to understand the pass-through tax loophole.
skip: The opening chit-chat about how hard government data is to use can be fast-forwarded; the core content starts at 11:16 with the explanation of pass-through.

points.h: Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
points.body: More than a decade ago, commissioned by the Treasury, the two authors linked corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because the IRS itself couldn't match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. That data project later became the basis of the book.

points.h: Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
points.body: Of pass-through business income, 70 cents of every dollar flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the rise in the top 1% income share came from pass-through business income. So there is no way to understand income inequality and wealth inequality without this sector. The authors had assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money; instead they found middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

points.h: Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
points.body: The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida held his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. Looking at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, the authors found car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

points.h: Car dealer wealth is half skill, half licence
points.body: The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a fine case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

points.h: Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
points.body: When you see a truck on the road with Budweiser on it, the truck actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores; state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at once. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up en masse in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

points.h: Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
points.body: The book contrasts two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, paying no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services such as doctors, carving out surgery, ancillary services or real estate can still shift more income into the lower-rate bucket.

points.h: A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
points.body: The authors say the reason the tax loophole survives so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he proposed together with Elizabeth Warren is funded by payroll taxes on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer claim the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

points.h: The owners' share of the pie rose from four-tenths to five-tenths
points.body: Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate: value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.
